faqs.q: What is High-Level Design (HLD) in a system design interview?
faqs.a: HLD is the architecture-level part of a system design round: you clarify requirements, estimate scale, define APIs and entities, choose databases, caches and queues, draw the end-to-end architecture and then defend the trade-offs and failure handling. This book teaches that flow with 19 worked case studies.

faqs.q: What is the difference between HLD and LLD?
faqs.a: HLD answers how a whole system scales: services, data stores, caching, messaging and consistency. faqs.q: What is the difference between Git and GitHub?
faqs.a: Git is a distributed version control system that runs on your computer and records the history of your files. GitHub is an online platform that hosts Git repositories and adds collaboration features such as pull requests, code review, Issues and GitHub Actions. You can use Git without GitHub, but GitHub is built on Git. Covered in Chapter 1.

faqs.q: What is the difference between git merge and git rebase?
faqs.a: git merge joins two branches and keeps their history as it happened, creating a merge commit unless a fast-forward is possible. git rebase replays your commits on top of another branch, giving a straight, linear history but creating new commit IDs. Avoid rebasing commits that others have already pulled. Covered in Chapters 8 and 9.

faqs.q: What is the difference between git reset and git revert?
faqs.a: git reset moves your branch back to an earlier commit and rewrites history (--soft keeps changes staged, --mixed keeps them unstaged, --hard discards them), so use it on local work. git revert adds a new commit that undoes an earlier one without rewriting history, so it is safe on shared branches. Covered in Chapter 6.

faqs.q: How do I recover a commit I lost after a reset?
faqs.a: Run git reflog to see every position HEAD has recently been at, find the commit hash from before the reset, then run git reset --hard <hash> or create a branch at it with git branch <name> <hash>. Covered in Chapter 6.

faqs.q: What does git push --force-with-lease do?
faqs.a: It force-pushes your branch only if the remote branch is still where you last saw it. If someone else pushed in the meantime, the push is refused instead of overwriting their work, which makes it safer than --force. Covered in Chapter 12.

faqs.q: What is the difference between git fetch and git pull?
faqs.a: git fetch downloads new commits from the remote and updates remote-tracking branches without touching your work. git pull runs a fetch and then merges (or rebases) those changes into your current branch. Covered in Chapter 12.

faqs.q: What is a detached HEAD in Git?
faqs.a: HEAD normally points to a branch. In a detached HEAD state it points straight at a commit, for example after checking out a tag or a commit hash. New commits made there belong to no branch, so create one with git switch -c <name> if you want to keep them. Covered in Chapters 3 and 7.

faqs.q: What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING?
faqs.a: WHERE filters individual rows before they are grouped, so it cannot use aggregates. HAVING filters whole groups after GROUP BY, so it can, for example HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2.

faqs.q: ROW_NUMBER vs RANK vs DENSE_RANK?
faqs.a: All three number rows in a window. ROW_NUMBER gives every row a unique number even on ties. RANK gives ties the same number and then skips (1, 2, 2, 4). DENSE_RANK gives ties the same number without gaps (1, 2, 2, 3), which is why it is used for the Nth highest salary.

faqs.q: Clustered vs non-clustered index?
faqs.a: A clustered index stores the table rows themselves in index order, so a table has at most one. A non-clustered index is a separate structure of keys pointing back to the rows; a table can have many, and a query it fully covers can be answered from the index alone.

faqs.q: Which isolation level prevents which anomaly?
faqs.a: READ COMMITTED prevents dirty reads. REPEATABLE READ also prevents non-repeatable reads. SERIALIZABLE prevents those plus phantoms and write skew. Higher levels are safer but block or abort more transactions.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a process and a thread?
faqs.a: A process is a program in execution with its own address space, files and resources. A thread is a unit of execution inside a process; threads of one process share its memory and files but each has its own stack, registers and program counter, so switching between them is cheaper.

faqs.q: What are the four conditions for deadlock?
faqs.a: Mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption and circular wait. A deadlock can happen only when all four hold at once, so breaking any one of them prevents it.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a mutex and a semaphore?
faqs.a: A mutex is a lock with ownership: only the thread that locked it can unlock it, and it protects one critical section. A semaphore is a counter that any thread can signal; a counting semaphore can let several threads in, which suits resource pools and producer-consumer.

faqs.q: What is thrashing?
faqs.a: Thrashing is when a process has too few frames, so it page-faults constantly and the system spends more time swapping pages than running code. CPU utilisation collapses; the fix is to give processes enough frames for their working set or run fewer of them.
